```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
ri <- function(x) knitr::inline_expr(x)
library(weft)
```

This article is for authors who already have weft turned on in a document
(see `vignette("weft", package = "weft")`) and want to print numbers, counts,
lists and dates the same way everywhere. After it you will know every
formatter class, the keys that adjust them, how weft rounds, what it does
with a missing value, and how to change the defaults for a project.

## Bare values and formatted values

A **bare value** is inline R with no attribute block:
`` `r ri("x")` ``. weft leaves it alone, and it prints exactly as knitr
prints it. weft still records it, and the static lints still count it as a
computed number.

A **formatted value** has an attribute block after the closing backtick, with
nothing in between: `` `r ri("x")`{.num} ``. The block holds one or more
**formatter classes**, and sometimes **keys** that adjust them. Under
Quarto, `` `{r} x`{.num} `` behaves the same.

## Where weft reads inline R

weft reads inline R wherever knitr evaluates it:

- in prose, headings, lists, tables and captions;
- inside a code span;
- inside a fenced block that is not a chunk;
- inside an HTML comment, closed or not;
- inside math and raw LaTeX.

It does not read a chunk's code, which is R and not text. Read there, inline
R counts as a value, the lints see it, and an attribute block after it formats
it. In the source below, `x` is `12.4567`, and the reader sees
`lm(y ~ 12.46)` in a code span:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Fit `lm(y ~ `r x`{.num})` to the data.
```

Two consequences follow, and both are because knitr does the same. Wrapping a
paragraph in an HTML comment does not switch its values or claims off, since
knitr still runs them, so the gate still counts them. And a fenced block
cannot show weft syntax literally: the inline R in it is evaluated. A
bracketed span (`[...]{.if ...}`) in a code span, a fence or a comment is left
as text.

Inline R in math is read and counted, and a class block after it writes TeX:
see "Values in math and raw LaTeX" below.

The examples below come from one document. Its data chunk is:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mean_ntu <- 8.2333
share <- 0.1234
p_val <- 0.0462
n_dry <- 0
n_wet <- 12
survey_no <- 3
record_years <- 11
sites <- c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower", "Estuary", "Mouth")
means <- c(Upper = 4.2, Middle = 7.9, Lower = 12.6)
depth_range <- c(0.4, 1.3)
visit <- as.Date("2024-09-02")
volume <- 1234567
flagged <- character(0)
```

## Numbers

```{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
Mean turbidity was `r mean_ntu`{.num}, or `r mean_ntu`{.num digits="2"} to
two places, or `r mean_ntu`{.num sigfig="1"} to one significant figure.

`r share`{.pct} of samples exceeded the guideline (`r p_val`{.p}).

The pond holds `r volume`{.num} L, `r volume`{.sci} L in scientific notation.
```

```text
Mean turbidity was 8.2, or 8.23 to two places, or 8 to one significant figure.

12.3% of samples exceeded the guideline (p = 0.046).

The pond holds 1,234,567 L, 1.2 × 10⁶ L in scientific notation.
```

| Class | Prints |
|---|---|
| `.num` | a number: a whole number with no decimals, any other to the default digits (one place unless set) |
| `.pct` | a proportion as a percentage: 0.1234 prints "12.3%" |
| `.sci` | scientific notation |
| `.p` | a p-value: "p = 0.046", "p < 0.001", "p > 0.99", never "p = 0.000" |
| `.date` | a date, in the default format "2 September 2024" |

`.num`, `.pct` and `.ord` put a thousands mark in numbers from 1,000 up. A
year held as a plain number gets one too, so print a year as a bare value,
or keep it in the dictionary as a `year` entry, which never gets a mark (see
`vignette("units", package = "weft")`):

```{r}
fmt_num(2024)
```

weft rounds half away from zero, on the number as written: 0.15 prints
"0.2". It prints the minus sign as the true minus (U+2212).

### A sign on a difference: `.plus`

A difference reads better with its sign. `.plus` prints `+` before a
number above zero:

```{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
The mean rose by `r d_mean`{.num .plus} mg/L (`r d_pct`{.pct .plus}).
The change ranged `r d_rng`{.range .plus} across sites.
```

```text
The mean rose by +1.2 mg/L (+12%).
The change ranged −0.5 to +1.2 across sites.
```

with `d_mean <- 1.2`, `d_pct <- 0.12` and `d_rng <- c(-0.5, 1.2)`. A
negative number keeps its minus. A number that prints as zero has no sign,
as it has no minus. Under `.range` the ends are joined by " to " when
either end has a sign, so no dash stands next to a sign:

```{r}
fmt_num(c(1.25, 0, -1.25), plus = TRUE)
fmt_range(c(1.2, 3.4), plus = TRUE)
fmt_range(c(0, 1.2), plus = TRUE)
```

`.plus` goes with `.num` or `.pct` (alone, it implies `.num`), with a list
class, and with `.a`: `` `r ri("8")`{.num .plus .a} `` prints "a +8". With
`.sci`, `.p`, `.date`, `.no`, a wording class or `.val`, or on an `n`,
`if`, `sign`, `list` or `cite` span, it is a construct error. No setting
signs every number: a sign belongs to a difference, and a project-wide
sign would print "+12 sites".

### p-values: `digits` and `label`

By default `.p` prints three decimals below 0.1 and two from 0.1 up, with
"p < 0.001" and "p > 0.99" at the ends. `digits` fixes the number of
decimals, and the ends move with it, so "p = 0.000" never prints:

```{r}
fmt_p(c(0.0004, 0.046, 0.12, 0.995))
fmt_p(c(0.0004, 0.046, 0.12, 0.9996), digits = 3)
fmt_p(c(0.004, 0.046, 0.995), digits = 2)
```

With `digits = 3`, a value below 0.001 prints "p < 0.001", a value that
would round to 1 prints "p > 0.999", and any other value prints with
exactly three decimals, trailing zeros kept: "p = 0.120". `digits` on `.p`
is a whole number from 1 to 6. `sigfig` on `.p` is a construct error.

`label` sets the text before the relation. Use it for an adjusted value,
or leave it empty to print the number alone:

```{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
The trend was weak (`r fit_p`{.p digits="3"}).
After correction it held (`r fit_q`{.p label="q"}).
Effects were small (`r fit_p`{.p label=""}).
```

```text
The trend was weak (p = 0.046).
After correction it held (q = 0.003).
Effects were small (0.046).
```

The label is printed as written, so `label="*p*"` prints an italic p.
`label` on anything but `.p` is a construct error. The settings
`p_digits` and `p_label` set both for a project, and a key on the value
wins over them.

## Counts and wording

```{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
`r n_dry`{.no .word .cap} sites were dry and `r n_wet`{.count} were wet.
This is the `r survey_no`{.ord} survey.

`r n_wet`{.word .cap} sites were wet. The logger gave
`r record_years`{.num .a}-year record.
```

```text
No sites were dry and 12 were wet. This is the 3rd survey.

Twelve sites were wet. The logger gave an 11-year record.
```

| Class | Prints |
|---|---|
| `.no` | a zero as "no" |
| `.word` | a whole number spelled out ("three"), in digits from 100 up |
| `.count` | a word below ten, digits from ten up ("three", "12") |
| `.ord` | an ordinal ("3rd") |
| `.a` | "a" or "an" before a number, by its sound ("an 11", "an 8") |
| `.cap` | a capital first letter |
| `.strong`, `.em` | bold or italic |

`.word`, `.count` and `.ord` need a whole number that is not negative. A
decimal or a negative number is a **value error**: the render fails at the
end and names the line.

## Lists

```{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
We sampled `r sites`{.and trunc="3"}, or `r sites`{.or sep="; "}.

Means were `r means`{.num .pairs}.

Depths ranged over `r depth_range`{.range} m. The first visit was on
`r visit`{.date}.

Flagged sites: `r flagged`{.and none="none"}.
```

```text
We sampled Upper, Middle, Lower and 2 others, or Upper; Middle; Lower;
Estuary or Mouth.

Means were Upper (4.2), Middle (7.9) and Lower (12.6).

Depths ranged over 0.4–1.3 m. The first visit was on 2 September 2024.

Flagged sites: none.
```

| Class | Prints |
|---|---|
| `.and`, `.or` | the items joined with "and" or "or" |
| `.pairs` | a named vector as "A (1.2), B (3.4) and C (5.6)" |
| `.range` | two numbers as a range ("3–5"), or "−5 to −3" when an end is negative or, with `.plus`, signed |
| `.ul`, `.ol`, `.dl` | a bullet list, a numbered list or a definition list |

A vector with no list class prints its items joined by ", ", as knitr
prints a vector.

`.ul`, `.ol` and `.dl` make a block, so the value must be alone in its
paragraph, and not inside a list item, a block quote or a table cell:

```{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
The sites were:

`r sites[1:3]`{.ul}
```

```text
The sites were:

- Upper
- Middle
- Lower
```

## Keys

Keys adjust a class. Write them inside the same attribute block, with the
value in double quotes.

| Key | Sets |
|---|---|
| `digits` | decimal places (on `.p`, a whole number from 1 to 6) |
| `sigfig` | significant figures (not with `digits`, not on `.p`) |
| `label` | the text before a p-value's relation, `.p` only |
| `unit` | the unit a quantity prints in (see the units article) |
| `sep` | the text between list items |
| `last` | the text before the last item |
| `trunc` | how many items to show before "and N others" |
| `none` | the text to print for an empty vector, with a list class |

`digits`, `sigfig` or `unit` on a value with no number class imply `.num`.

## Combining classes

Classes act in four fixed stages, whatever order you write them in:

1. **Number**: at most one of `.num`, `.pct`, `.sci`, `.p`, `.date`;
   and `.plus`, which is in no group.
2. **Wording**: `.no`, then at most one of `.word`, `.count`, `.ord`.
3. **List**: at most one of `.and`, `.or`, `.pairs`, `.range`, `.ul`,
   `.ol`, `.dl`.
4. **Text**: `.a`, then `.cap`, then `.strong` or `.em`.

So `{.num .pairs}` formats each number and then pairs them, and
`{.no .word .cap}` turns 0 into "no", then capitalises it. Two classes from
one "at most one" group are a **construct error**, which stops the render at
once and which the lints report without running anything.

A class or key that weft does not own passes through to a Pandoc span around
the output. `weft_str()`, described below, shows the markdown weft writes:

```{r}
mean_ntu <- 8.2333
weft_str("Turbidity was `r mean_ntu`{.num .strong} and `r mean_ntu`{.num .smallcaps}.")
```

A misspelt class, such as `.nmu`, is therefore not an error. The tier-2 lint
`name` lists it (see `vignette("lints", package = "weft")`).

## Numbers that print as zero

A number that is not zero but rounds to "0.0" under the default digits is
easy to miss. weft prints it, and records a **warned check**: the render
does not fail, and the warning is printed at the end of the knit. Outside a
knit it is an R warning:

```{r}
fmt_num(0.04)
fmt_num(0.04, sigfig = 1)
fmt_num(0.04, digits = 1)
```

Give `sigfig` to show the number, or `digits` to say that the zero is
what you meant. Either one silences the warning.

## Missing values

`NA`, `NaN`, `Inf`, `-Inf` and a vector of length zero are **missing
values**. Given to a formatter, a span or a phrase function, a missing value
is a "no value" failure: the render fails at the end, and in draft mode the
value prints as `<<weft: no value, line N>>`. A bare value with no attribute
block prints `NA` as knitr does, but a bare value whose printed text is
exactly `NA`, `NaN`, `Inf` or `-Inf` is a warned check: the render does not
fail, `last_knit()$warnings` holds a row for it, and the condition log
records a warning of class `weft_bare_missing_warning`. A vector such as
`c(1, NA)` records nothing. Set `bare_missing: false` in `_weft.yml` to turn
the check off.

A list class with `none` is the exception: an empty vector prints the
`none` text, as in the "Flagged sites" example above.

## Formatters in R code

Every class `.x` has a function `fmt_x()`, for chunks, plot labels and
table cells:

```{r}
fmt_num(8.2333, digits = 2)
fmt_pct(0.1234)
fmt_p(0.00002)
fmt_word(3)
fmt_count(c(3, 12))
fmt_ord(3)
fmt_and(c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower", "Estuary"), trunc = 2)
fmt_range(c(-5, -3))
fmt_date(as.Date("2024-09-02"))
fmt_cap(fmt_word(12))
fmt_a(fmt_num(11))
```

A formatter returns a `weft_text`: a character vector that carries its
**printed record**, the number as printed, whether decimals show, and
whether it is a bound such as "< 0.01". Pass one formatter's result to
another and the record goes with it:

```{r}
fmt_pairs(fmt_num(c(Upper = 4.2, Middle = 7.9, Lower = 12.6)))
```

`glue_vec()` is the joining engine behind `.and` and `.or`:

```{r}
glue_vec(c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower"), last = " or ")
```

`weft_str()` resolves weft markup in a string, for text that no chunk option
reaches: a `kable()` caption, a plot title, text written by a chunk with
`results: asis`.

```{r}
n_sites <- 3
weft_str("Turbidity at `r n_sites`{.word} sites, mean `r mean_ntu`{.num} NTU.")
```

## Captions and front matter

A construct works in a chunk's caption. Write the caption as a YAML block
scalar (`|`), because a construct in any other form of scalar is a construct
error:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
```{r}
#| label: fig-depth
#| fig-cap: |
#|   Depth at [a site | # sites]{n="n_sites"}, mean `r mean(d)`{.num} m.
d <- c(0.4, 0.7, 1.3)
n_sites <- length(d)
barplot(d)
```
````

The caption is resolved after the chunk runs, so it sees objects the chunk
made. The same works in `fig-alt`, `fig-subcap` and `tbl-cap` under Quarto,
and in `fig.cap` and `fig.alt` under R Markdown. A construct in the caption
of a chunk with `cache: true` or `eval: false` is a construct error: write
that caption in a figure div instead.

The front-matter fields `title`, `subtitle`, `abstract` and `description`
take constructs too, when written as a block scalar. Front matter is read
before any chunk runs, so a field that needs a chunk's values goes in a
second metadata block at the end of the document:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
abstract: |
  We sampled [a site | # sites]{n="n_sites"}, to a mean depth of
  `r mean(d)`{.num} m.
---
````

## Values in math and raw LaTeX

A formatter's markdown is wrong inside a formula. `.sci` would write a
markdown superscript, `.pct` a bare `%` that TeX reads as a comment, and the
comma in `1,234` would be spaced as punctuation. So in math and raw LaTeX a
class block writes TeX. Write the value as inline R with a class block, as in
prose:

```{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
The fit gave $a = `r mean_ntu`{.num digits=2}$ and $b = `r share`{.pct}$.

$$ V = `r volume`{.sci} $$
```

weft puts this into the document before the renderer sees it:

```text
The fit gave $a = 8.23$ and $b = 12.3\%$.

$$ V = 1.2 \times 10^{6} $$
```

and the renderer sets it as math, so the page shows a = 8.23, b = 12.3% and
V = 1.2 × 10⁶.

These places count as math: `$...$`, `$$...$$`, the math environments of LaTeX
(`equation`, `align`, `gather`, `multline`, `cases`, the matrices and the
others, starred or not) and, in an `.Rmd` knitted with R Markdown, `\(...\)`
and `\[...\]`. Under Quarto those two forms are not math, and weft does not
treat them as math. Raw LaTeX is any other `\begin{...}` environment, a fence
written ```` ```{=latex} ```` or ```` ```{=tex} ````, and a code span followed
by `{=latex}` or `{=tex}`. A `{=typst}` or `{=html}` fence is neither, and
keeps the markdown of prose. A raw command such as `\textbf{...}` in the middle
of a paragraph is not found.

### What each class prints

With the values of the document above (`depth_range` is `c(0.4, 1.3)`), in
math:

| Written | Prints, as TeX |
|---|---|
| `` `r ri("mean_ntu")`{.num} `` | `8.2` |
| `` `r ri("volume")`{.num} `` | `1{,}234{,}567` |
| `` `r ri("share")`{.pct} `` | `12.3\%` |
| `` `r ri("share")`{.pct .plus} `` | `+12.3\%` |
| `` `r ri("p_val")`{.p} `` | `p = 0.046` |
| `` `r ri("volume")`{.sci} `` | `1.2 \times 10^{6}` |
| `` `r ri("depth_range")`{.range} `` | `0.4\ \text{to}\ 1.3` |

`.p` writes its label, so a formula holds `` `r ri("p_val")`{.p} `` alone, and
not `p =` before it. The minus sign is always `-`, whatever the `minus` setting
says. The thousands mark is `{,}`, which keeps the comma from taking
punctuation spacing. A range always says "to", even between two positive
numbers: no dash survives every renderer, and a dash between numbers in a
formula reads as a subtraction. The other marks follow your settings, in TeX:
`big_mark: " "` prints `1\,234\,567`, and `p_label: "adj. p"` prints
`\text{adj. p}`. A `label` key on `.p` is TeX already and goes in as you write
it: `label="\tilde{p}"` prints `\tilde{p} = 0.046`.

A value with a unit prints the unit inside `\text{}`: `5\,\text{mg/L}`,
`5\,\text{m}^{2}`, `20\,\text{°C}`. The characters of a unit, such as the degree
and micro signs, go through unchanged. `.uname` prints the name,
`5\ \text{milligrams per litre}`.

### What is refused, and why

A formula holds numbers. The classes that print words, emphasis or a list have
no TeX form, and in math and raw LaTeX they are a construct error:

- `.word`, `.count`, `.ord`, `.no`, `.date`, `.a` and `.cap` print words.
- `.em` and `.strong` are markdown emphasis. Put `\mathbf{}` or `\mathit{}`
  round the value in the formula.
- `.and`, `.or`, `.pairs`, `.ul`, `.ol` and `.dl`, and the keys `sep`, `last`,
  `trunc` and `none`, join items. Use `.range` for two ends.

So is a class or key that is not weft's, because weft would put the value in a
Pandoc span, and a formula has none. `lints()` finds these without running R,
and a render stops at one. The message names the class and says why.

### In raw LaTeX

In raw LaTeX the output of a construct is wrapped in `\ensuremath{...}`, so it
is safe in running text as well as in a math mode:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
```{=latex}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
Share & `r share`{.pct} \\
\end{tabular}
```
````

writes `\ensuremath{12.3\%}` into the cell. A failure marker is written inside
`\text{}`, and in raw LaTeX inside the wrapper too.

A **bare value**, inline R with no class block, is left as it is everywhere.
In math it prints as knitr prints it. In raw LaTeX it is not wrapped, so a
string in a `tabular` cell stays text. Writing `fmt_num(x)` in a bare value in
math therefore writes markdown, which is the fault the class block removes: the
`value-format` lint says so, and suggests the class block.

### From code

Every `fmt_*()` takes `target` as its last argument. `"markdown"` is the default
and the output you know. `target = "tex"` writes the TeX of this section, for
text you build in code and put into a formula:

```{r}
fmt_num(1234567, target = "tex")
fmt_pct(0.1234, target = "tex")
fmt_range(c(0.4, 1.3), target = "tex")
fmt_num(u(5, mg/L), target = "tex")
```

A text made for TeX carries the attribute `target = "tex"`. Passing it to a
markdown formatter is an error, because it would print TeX source in a
paragraph: format the number again, without `target`. The functions that print
words, emphasis or a list refuse `target = "tex"`, as the classes are refused
in math, and any other value of `target` is an error too.

### Project formatters in math

A project formatter writes markdown. To use it in math it must say that it can
write TeX, with `targets:` in its registration:

```yaml
formatters:
  .millions:
    function: in_millions
    stage: number
    targets: [markdown, tex]
```

```r
in_millions <- function(x, target = "markdown") {
  txt <- paste(weft::fmt_num(x / 1e6, target = target), "million")
  if (target == "tex") paste0("\\text{", txt, "}") else txt
}
```

`targets:` is `[markdown]` unless set, and must include `markdown`. A function
that lists `tex` is called with `target = "markdown"` or `target = "tex"` as its
last argument, after any options, and must take `target` or `...`. A class that
does not list `tex` is a construct error in math.

## Changing the defaults

Project settings live in `_weft.yml` at the project root. A document
overrides them with a `weft:` key in its own front matter. The settings for
values are:

| Setting | Default | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| `digits` | `1` | decimal places for a number that is not whole |
| `decimal_mark` | `"."` | the decimal mark |
| `big_mark` | `","` | the thousands mark |
| `thousands_from` | `1000` | the smallest number that gets a thousands mark |
| `serial_comma` | `false` | a comma before the final "and" or "or" of three or more items |
| `minus` | `"−"` | the minus sign |
| `pct_proportion` | `true` | whether `.pct` reads 0.12 as 12% |
| `p_digits` | `null` | the decimals of `.p`, 1 to 6; `null` keeps the default rule |
| `p_label` | `"p"` | the text before a p-value's relation; may be `""` |
| `count_threshold` | `10` | where `.count` switches from words to digits |
| `word_limit` | `100` | where `.word` switches to digits |
| `date_format` | `"%-d %B %Y"` | the format of `.date` |
| `governor_class` | `.num` | the class that formats the number of an `n` or `sign` span |
| `bare_missing` | `true` | whether a bare value that prints a missing value is a warned check |

With this `_weft.yml`:

```yaml
digits: 2
serial_comma: true
count_threshold: 20
formatters:
  .millions:
    function: in_millions
    stage: number
```

and this document:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
title: "Settings"
output: html_document
knitr:
  opts_knit:
    weft: !expr weft::weft_setup()
weft:
  date_format: "%d/%m/%Y"
---

```{r data}
in_millions <- function(x) paste(format(round(x / 1e6, 1), nsmall = 1), "million")
mean_ntu <- 8.2333
n_wet <- 12
sites <- c("Upper", "Middle", "Lower")
visit <- as.Date("2024-09-02")
volume <- 1234567
```

Mean turbidity was `r mean_ntu`{.num}. `r n_wet`{.count .cap} sites were wet:
`r sites`{.and}. The first visit was on `r visit`{.date}. The pond holds
`r volume`{.millions} litres.
````

the paragraph renders as:

```text
Mean turbidity was 8.23. Twelve sites were wet: Upper, Middle, and Lower.
The first visit was on 02/09/2024. The pond holds 1.2 million litres.
```

The `formatters:` setting registers a **project formatter**: a class name,
the function behind it (`pkg::fun`, or a name the document can see), and the
stage it acts in (`number` unless given). It counts towards that stage's "at
most one" rule, and it may not reuse the name of a weft class. A formatter that
is to be used in math lists `targets: [markdown, tex]` as well (see "Project
formatters in math" above).

### Options for a project formatter

A project formatter can take **options**: keys written on the construct that
reach the function as named arguments. Declare them under `options:`, each
with a type:

```yaml
formatters:
  .millions:
    function: in_millions
    stage: number
    options:
      digits: integer
      word: string
```

```r
in_millions <- function(x, digits = NULL, word = "million") {
  paste(weft::fmt_num(x / 1e6, digits = digits), word)
}
```

`` `r ri("volume")`{.millions digits=2} `` then prints "1.23 million" and
`` `r ri("volume")`{.millions word="M"} `` prints "1.2 M". The function gets only
the options the construct writes, in the order `options:` lists them, so its
own defaults apply to the rest. Give a forwarded option a `NULL` default, as
`digits` has here, and the project's `digits` setting still applies when the
construct writes none. A formatter with no `options:` is called with the value
alone, as before.

The types are `number`, `integer`, `string` and `logical`. A value is read by
its type and arrives as a number, a whole number, a string exactly as written,
or `TRUE` or `FALSE` (written `true` or `false`, in any case). A value outside
its type is a construct error, found when the document is scanned. A list of
names (`options: [digits, word]`) declares each as a string, except that a weft
key of the formatter's stage (`digits` and `sigfig` for a number formatter,
`sep`, `last` and `trunc` for a collapse formatter) keeps its own type. The
function must have an argument for every declared option, or `...`, and no
option may share the name of its first argument, which receives the value;
weft says so when the formatter runs.

What happens to a key that is not declared:

- A weft key of the formatter's stage is an error. `{.millions digits=2}` with
  no `digits` declared stops the render, where `digits` was once dropped
  without a word. Declare it, or remove it.
- Any other key passes through to the output as an attribute, as it does on a
  weft class. `lints()` points out a name that is one edit from an option, and
  an option of another formatter.
- A declared option is yours: it is not passed through, and its letter case
  does not matter.

A later `formatters:` entry for the same class, in a document's front matter,
replaces `options:` as a whole. The names `n`, `if`, `sign`, `list`, `cite`,
`unit`, `none`, `label`, `why`, `decision`, `claim`, `level` and `target` are
weft's and cannot be options. Options are for R documents; a named value on
the Lua filter route cannot take a project formatter.
